title: Habakkuk 3:16–19
context: The psalm ends with Habakkuk’s response to the vision. He trembles in body and voice, yet resolves to “wait quietly for the day of trouble,” the coming of the invader (3:16). Then comes the book’s best-known confession: even if the fig tree, the vine, the olive, the fields, the flocks, and the herds all fail, “yet I will rejoice in the LORD” (3:17–18). God, the Lord, is his strength, making his feet like deer’s feet on the heights (3:19; compare Psalm 18:33). The final line, “For the music director, on my stringed instruments,” is a musical notation like those that head many psalms; here it stands at the close. The prophet who began by asking “how long” ends in joy without any change in circumstances. This passage is shared ground: both traditions read it as faith that rejoices in God himself when outward blessing fails, and both see it as the fulfillment of the call in 2:4 to live by faith.

verses.text: I heard, and my body trembled. My lips quivered at the voice. Rottenness enters into my bones, and I tremble in my place because I must wait quietly for the day of trouble, for the coming up of the people who invade us.
verses.arminianNotes: “I heard, and my body trembled.” Habakkuk responds physically to the vision. Arminian readers value the honesty: faith does not remove fear, but it chooses to “wait quietly for the day of trouble,” trusting God through what is coming.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the trembling as the right response to God’s majesty, and the quiet waiting as submission to his appointed time (compare 2:3). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as faith that feels terror yet waits, and both note that “the people who invade us” most likely refers to the Babylonian invasion, though the verse does not name them.

verses.text: For even though the fig tree doesn’t flourish, nor fruit be in the vines, the labor of the olive fails, the fields yield no food, the flocks are cut off from the fold, and there is no herd in the stalls,
verses.arminianNotes: “For even though the fig tree doesn’t flourish, nor fruit be in the vines.” Arminian readers see faith that holds firm when every sign of blessing fails, a costly trust in God rather than in his gifts.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the loss of crops and flocks as within God’s providence, perhaps the result of invasion, and faith clinging to God himself. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as describing total agricultural failure, whether from war or other causes, and both see it as the setting for the most striking confession in the book.

verses.text: yet I will rejoice in the LORD. I will be joyful in the God of my salvation!
verses.arminianNotes: “yet I will rejoice in the LORD. I will be joyful in the God of my salvation!” Arminian readers see joy as a resolute act of faith, rooted not in circumstances but in God, and offered to him when nothing else remains.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see such joy as the fruit of grace, God’s own work in his people, and the culmination of the righteous living by faith (2:4). Shared ground: this verse is common ground; both traditions read it as joy in God himself rather than in his gifts, and both treat it as a model for believers who face loss.

verses.text: GOD, the Lord, is my strength. He makes my feet like deer’s feet, and enables me to go in high places. For the music director, on my stringed instruments.
verses.arminianNotes: “GOD, the Lord, is my strength. He makes my feet like deer’s feet.” Arminian readers see God’s enabling strength allowing the believer to walk securely on hard terrain, an image shared with Psalm 18:33.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God as the source of all strength and steadfastness, bringing his people safely “in high places.” Shared ground: both traditions read the closing image as confidence in God’s sustaining power, and both note that the final line, “For the music director, on my stringed instruments,” is a musical notation like those in the Psalms.
